analysis.background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens (A1) and molecular surveillance of hosts and their ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife‑ectoparasite interface (A2).
analysis.methods: From 2022‑2025, 1444 wild small mammals and 12,869 chigger mites (pooled into 680 host‑associated pools) were collected at 17 sites in South Korea (A3); liver samples and mite pools were screened for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR/RT‑PCR followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses (A4).
analysis.results: Apodemus agrarius accounted for 84.9% of captures (A5). Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA was detected in 69.6% of mite pools, while B. bacilliformis, B. henselae, and B. taylorii each appeared in 0.2% of mammal liver samples (A6). Coxiella burnetii DNA was found in 3.5% of liver samples, all from autumn 2024 (A7). Orthohantavirus RNA was identified in 2.6% of small mammals, predominantly A. agrarius (94.6%) and in 0.4% of mite pools (A8‑A10).
analysis.contribution: The findings provide the first molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in host‑associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small‑mammal liver samples in South Korea, offering descriptive baseline data for wildlife‑based molecular surveillance (A11‑A15).
analysis.limitations: The abstract does not establish seasonal patterns, individual‑mite infection prevalence, or vector competence, and only abstract information is available (A16).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens, and molecular surveillance of hosts and ectoparasites can reveal pathogen presence at the wildlife‑ectoparasite interface. Methods: Between 2022‑2025, 1444 wild small mammals and 12,869 chigger mites (pooled into 680 pools) were collected from 17 sites in South Korea; liver samples and mite pools were screened for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses by PCR/RT‑PCR and sequencing. Results: Apodemus agrarius comprised 84.9% of captures. Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA was found in 69.6% of mite pools; B. bacilliformis, B. henselae, and B. taylorii each appeared in 0.2% of mammal livers. Coxiella burnetii DNA occurred in 3.5% of livers (all autumn 2024). Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 2.6% of mammals, mainly A. agrarius (94.6%), and in 0.4% of mite pools. Contribution: First molecular evidence of B. schoenbuchensis in chigger mites and first report of B. bacilliformis and B. henselae DNA in Korean wild mammals, providing baseline surveillance data. Limitations: The abstract lacks detailed seasonal or individual‑mite prevalence data and does not assess vector competence; only abstract information is available.

papers.title_zh: 在韩国野生小型哺乳动物及其相关恙螨中对巴尔通体属、Coxiella burnetii和正汉坦病毒进行分子监测。

analysis_zh.background: 野生小型哺乳动物是多种人畜共患病原体的重要宿主 (A1),对宿主及其外寄生虫进行分子监测可提供野生动物‐外寄生虫界面病原体检测信息 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 2022‐2025 年期间,在韩国 17 个地点采集了 1444 只野生小型哺乳动物和 12,869 只恙螨(合并为 680 个宿主相关池) (A3);对肝脏样本和恙螨池进行 Bartonella 属、Coxiella burnetii 和 正汉坦病毒 的 PCR/RT‐PCR 检测,随后进行序列和系统发育分析 (A4)。
analysis_zh.results: Apodemus agrarius 占捕获总数的 84.9% (A5)。在恙螨池中检测到 Bartonella schoenbuchensis DNA,检出率为 69.6%;而 B. bacilliformis、B. henselae 和 B. taylorii 各出现在 0.2% 的哺乳动物肝脏样本中 (A6)。Coxiella burnetii DNA 在 3.5% 的肝脏样本中检出,全部来自 2024 年秋季 (A7)。正汉坦病毒 RNA 在 2.6% 的小型哺乳动物中被鉴定,主要为 A. agrarius(占 94.6%),在恙螨池中的检出率为 0.4% (A8‐A10)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究首次在宿主相关恙螨池中提供 B. schoenbuchensis 的分子证据,并记录了在韩国野生小型哺乳动物肝脏样本中此前未报告的 B. bacilliformis 和 B. henselae DNA,为基于野生动物的分子监测提供了描述性基线数据 (A11‐A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 摘要未确定季节性模式、单个恙螨感染率或媒介能力,且仅提供摘要信息 (A16)。

papers.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the 34 modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments 35 in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, 36 are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better 37 understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between 38 organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural 39 hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends 40 on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at 41 different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA- 42 sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by 43 three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from 44 bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. 45 Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific 46 regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the 47 complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate 48 immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways. 49 50 Introduction 51 Orthohantaviruses (1) are found in small mammals, such as rodents, shrews, moles 52 and bats. Their long co-evolution with these globally distributed host species (2-4) 53 3 accounts for their presence in all continents (5). These viruses do not cause apparent 54 diseases in their natural hosts. Currently, only rodent-borne orthohantaviruses are 55 known to be pathogenic in humans, mainly through the inhalation of aerosols from 56 contaminated animal excreta. After entering the respiratory tract, orthohantaviruses 57 cross the pulmonary epithelial barrier and disseminate throughout the body by 58 infecting vascular endothelial cells and monocytes (6, 7). In humans, an exacerbated 59 immune response (8) leads to hemorrhagic fevers with renal syndromes (HFRS) and 60 nephropathia epidemica (NE) in the Old World (9), or to hantavirus cardio-pulmonary 61 syndromes (HCPS) in the Americas (10). The activation of innate immunity to 62 eliminate viruses, and the viral strategies to counteract it, vary depending on the 63 orthohantavirus species (11). Sustained interferon (IFN) activation may contribute to 64 inflammatory responses that influence viral pathogenicity (12). 65 We previously showed that the pathogenic Puumala virus (PUUV), the weakly 66 pathogenic Tula virus (TULV) and the non-pathogenic Prospect Hill virus (PHV), 67 differentially regulate IFN responses in human and rodent cells (13, 14). Myodes 68 glareolus (bank vole) is the natural host of PUUV, whereas TULV and PHV naturally 69 infect Microtus arvalis (common vole) and Microtus pensylvanicus (eastern meadow 70 vole), respectively. These orthohantaviruses exhibit different replication 71 characteristics in bank voles-derived cells. These differences correlate with cellular 72 restrictions acting at distinct stages of the viral cycle from entry to replication and viral 73 release (14). In human cells, type I and III IFNs and several IFN stimulated genes 74 (ISGs) are strongly activated by PUUV and PHV but not by TULV. In contrast, bank 75 vole cells display a delayed and weaker IFN response. 76 Despite advances in our understanding of the regulation of host responses in 77 rodents, the mechanisms leading to the differential outcomes of orthohantavirus 78 4 infection in their natural hosts remain poorly understood (15-18). To explore this 79 question, we compared gene expression profiles induced by PUUV, TULV and PHV. 80 Building on the opportunity that the recent availability of an updated Myodes 81 glareolus genome assembly in the NCBI database (GCF_902806735.1) provides, we 82 performed transcriptomic analysis by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of bank vole 83 epithelial cells derived from the kidneys (MyglaSWRecB) and the respiratory tract 84 (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) infected with these different orthohantaviruses. 85 Differential gene expression and pathway analyses revealed virus- and tissue- 86 specific regulatory programs that likely contribute to distinct infection outcomes and 87 host–virus interactions. 88 89 Material and methods 90 Cells and viruses 91 The three bank vole cells lines, MyglaSWRecB, MyglaSWTrach, MyglaAEC, 92 originated from kidney, tracheal and alveolar lung epithelium, respectively, and were 93 SV40 T antigen-immortalized (19). Cells were grown at 37°C with 5% CO2 in DMEM 94 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% of heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum 95 (Biosera). 96 Puumala Sotkamo viral strain (PUUV) and Prospect Hill viral strain (PHV) were 97 provided by Andreas Rang (Charité University, Berlin). Tula Moravia virus (TULV) 98 was obtained from Alexander Plyusnin (Helsinki University). Viral stocks were 99 propagated on Vero E6 cells as previously described (14). 100 RNA preparation, sequencing and transcriptomic analysis 101 RNA preparation from infected cells was performed as previously described (14). 102 Briefly, bank vole cells were infected with orthohantaviruses at a multiplicity of 103 5 infection (MOI) of 0.5. Total RNA was extracted 5 days post infection (dpi). After 104 washing with PBS, cells were treated with Trizol (Tri Reagent, Sigma Aldrich) and 105 chloroform. The aqueous phase containing the RNA was precipitated with 106 isopropanol and resuspended in distilled water. RNA concentration was measured 107 using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Four biological replicates 108 were generated for each condition: non-infected controls (NI) and cells infected with 109 PUUV, PHV or TULV orthohantaviruses. 110 Strand-specific single-end cDNA libraries were prepared from total RNA using 111 the Illumina Stranded mRNA prep, ligation preparation kit (Illumina) according to the 112 manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 113 platform. 114 RNA-seq analyses were performed using the Sequana framework, v0.14.1 (20). 115 Viral infection in samples was first verified using the Sequana mapper workflow to 116 detect specific viral RNA sequences. Transcriptomic analysis was conducted using 117 the Sequana RNA-seq pipeline (v0.15.2), implemented in Snakemake (21) and 118 available at https://github.com/sequana/sequana_RNA-seq, using default 119 parameters. Adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed with fastp v0.20.1 120 (22). Cleaned reads were aligned with STAR (23) against the Myodes glareolus 121 reference genome assembly GCA_902806735.1 and the Mus musculus reference 122 genome (GRCm38/mm10). Library strandedness was automatically inferred by the 123 pipeline, and gene-level counts were generated using FeatureCounts (package 124 Subread v2.0.1). Differential gene expression analysis was performed from the count 125 matrix using DESeq2 (v1.38.2) with R v4.2.1. Statistical significance was assessed 126 using Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values with a false discovery rate (FDR) 127 threshold of 0.05. 128 6 All third-party software dependencies were executed within containerized 129 environments provided through the Damona project (https://damona.readthedocs.io), 130 ensuring reproducibility. 131 Visualization of differentially expressed genes 132 Venn diagrams were drawn using the online Venny 2.1 program, an interactive tool 133 for comparing lists with Venn's diagrams (24) allowing the determination of the 134 number and identification of genes common or specific to a given situation. Volcano 135 plots and gene comparison representations were obtained using GraphPad Prism 11. 136 Heatmaps representations of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were 137 generated using the pheatmap function in the R program. This analysis was 138 performed for tracheal cells infected with PUUV, PHV, or TULV across the bank vole 139 and mouse reference genomes (BV and mm10). For each condition, only one entry 140 per gene was retained, prioritizing the lowest adjusted p-value (padj) and, in case of 141 ties, the largest absolute log2FoldChange. For the relative representation of genes 142 identified through the BV genome in comparison to the mm10 genome specifically in 143 infected tracheal cells, the six DEGs tables were merged by gene union, with missing 144 values replaced by zero. Genes with non-finite values (NA, NaN, Inf) or zero variance 145 across conditions were removed. Up and downregulated genes were defined based 146 on the sign of the mean log2FoldChange across the six conditions. Heatmaps were 147 generated using pheatmap in R, scaling values by gene (scale = "row"), clustering 148 columns using Euclidean distance and complete linkage, and annotating columns by 149 virus and genome. This approach enabled visualization of global expression profiles 150 and comparison of regulatory patterns across viruses and genomes. 151 Pathway enrichment 152 7 Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was 153 performed using DAVID Bioinformatics Resources v6.8 154 (https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/tools.jsp) (Database for Annotation, Visualization 155 and Integrated Discovery (25). Official gene symbols were submitted for annotation 156 clustering and enrichment analyses of Gene Ontology (GO) terms, KEGG and 157 Reactome pathways, and InterPro protein domains. The background dataset was set 158 to the entire Mus musculus genome, and Enriched terms were considered 159 statistically significant based on a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05. 160 Data availability 161 The RNA-seq data set 1 was published in (14) with accession GSE198751. The 162 RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 were deposited to ENA (accession E-MTAB-16656). 163 164 Results 165 Quantitative gene regulation in kidney cells or in respiratory cells varies 166 depending on orthohantavirus species 167 To evaluate the effect of orthohantavirus infection on gene expression, different 168 epithelial bank vole (BV) cell lines derived from organs targeted by these viruses, 169 such as the respiratory tract (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) and the kidneys 170 (MyglaSWRecB), were infected at a MOI of 0.5 with PUUV, TULV or PHV and their 171 RNAs extracted five days post infection (5 dpi). At this time point, the viral replication 172 of PUUV and PHV is clearly detectable and constitutes a suitable basis for the 173 quantitative and qualitative characterization of gene expression by RNA-seq, as 174 previously described (14). The experimental approach is schematized in Figure 1. 175 The RNA-seq generated a similar number of reads (20-30 million) to each sample 176 and these samples are clustered according to infection status distinguishing 177 8 uninfected and infected conditions (Fig. SD1). The number of identified genes 178 significantly upregulated and downregulated (FC>2 and <-2, p-value <0.05), varied 179 according to the virus and cell types (Table 1). Venn diagrams illustrate, in addition to 180 the number of genes, the percentage of genes specific or common to different 181 situations. Since few genes were upregulated upon orthohantavirus infection of 182 pulmonary alveolar MyglaAEC#2 cells (Table 1), they were not included in Venn 183 diagrams and volcano plot representations. Around 70% of differentially expressed 184 genes (DEGs), were upregulated and 30% were downregulated. However, more 185 genes appeared differentially expressed (DE) in the infected tracheal cells than in the 186 kidney cells, both with PUUV (308 vs 66, Fig. 2A) and PHV (545 vs 254, Fig. 2B). 187 Strikingly, few DEGs were common to these two cell lines upon PUUV infection 188 (1.1%) or PHV infection (8.1%). In the case of TULV (Table 1) very few genes were 189 DE in MyglaSWRecB compared to what is seen in MyglaSWTrach (4 vs 509). 190 While TULV did not induce significant gene regulation in the kidney cell line, 191 PUUV and PHV did (Fig. 3A). Indeed, in MyglaSWRecB cells, 37 of 66 genes (56%) 192 were specifically regulated by PUUV, and 226 of 254 genes (88.9.%) by PHV. This 193 represented 12.5% and 76.6% of the total identified genes for PUUV and PHV 194 respectively, when only 9.5% of genes were common to PUUV- and PHV-infected 195 cells. In the tracheal cells, MyglaSWTrach, the situation was quite different (Fig 3B). 196 Many more genes were DE upon infection with the nonpathogenic orthohantaviruses, 197 PHV (545) and TULV (509), than with PUUV (308). Among these genes, only 10.5% 198 were specific to PUUV infection, 21.6% to PHV infection and 15.4% to TULV 199 infection. Interestingly, in this cell line, a higher proportion of DEGs was shared 200 following infection with all three orthohantaviruses (21.2%) or with the non- 201 pathogenic heterologous orthohantaviruses PHV and TULV (23.7%). In contrast, 202 9 fewer genes were common to PUUV and PHV or PUUV and TULV (3.1% and 4;6% 203 respectively). Although the volcano plots show gene expression levels 204 (log2FoldChange) and their significance (-log10_adjusted p-value), it should be noted 205 that more genes were upregulated than downregulated in each situation (Fig. 3C). 206 Due to the limited information available for the bank vole genome, our previous 207 work identified DEGs in infected renal cells from the mouse database (mm10). 208 Therefore, the RNA-seq data generated in the present study were also analyzed 209 against this mouse database. The percentage of DEGs found in infected tracheal 210 (Fig. SD2A) or renal (Fig. SD3A) cells, specific or common to different viruses was 211 similar, whether using the bank vole or the mouse reference genome. However, it is 212 worth noting that for PUUV, PHV and TULV, only about 20% of the identified genes in 213 MyglaSWTrach cells were found with the two genomes (Fig. SD2B), highlighting the 214 importance of combining the two analyses. The same observation was made for the 215 renal cells (Fig. SD3B), where an even smaller percentage of genes appeared 216 common to the two databases. This result should nevertheless be viewed with 217 caution due to the small number of DEGs identified after PUUV infection of 218 MyglaSWRecB cells. Therefore, all the annotated genes found in the mouse and vole 219 reference genomes were compiled into a single list of identification (Table 2 and 220 Table SD). It should also be noted that many genes annotated as genomic loci (Loc 221 genes) have orthologues in the mouse or human genome. This is for instance the 222 case for 25, 54 and 42 Loc genes (FC>4 and <-4), for PUUV, PHV and TULV 223 respectively in tracheal infected cells, and for 7 and 72 genes, for PUUV and PHV in 224 renal infected cells. The putative corresponding names of these identified sequences 225 have been added to the tables (in blue) and when several sequences referred to a 226 similar orthologue, only the one with the highest FC value was retained. 227 10 Innate immune responses are activated by orthohantaviruses in kidney and 228 respiratory epithelial cells from bank vole 229 We compared the DEGs identified in the renal and the tracheal cell lines infected with 230 the different orthohantaviruses, PUUV, PHV, TULV, using the bank vole and the 231 mouse reference genomes (Table 2). The transcripts regulated by one or more 232 viruses in different BV cell lines (Fig. 4A) were mainly involved in antiviral defense as 233 expected following the recognition of RNA viruses by Toll-, Nod- or Rig1-like 234 receptors (TLR, NLR, RLR) upstream of innate immune responses (12). Only two 235 genes were significantly activated by PUUV (FC>2) in both MyglaSWTrach and 236 MyglaSWRecB cell lines; Ddx60, a helicase promoting RLR signaling, and the IFN- 237 inducible gene Ifit1, known to inhibit viral replication (26). These two genes were also 238 upregulated by PHV in these two BV cell lines. It is remarkable that only a few ISGs 239 were slightly upregulated by PUUV, the orthohantavirus specifically transmitted by 240 bank voles, as compared with the much stronger induction observed following 241 infection with the heterologous orthohantavirus PHV. papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by HV remains a serious threat to global public health security, with its epidemic scope continuing to expand. After more than 20 years of application in China, HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) has been proven to effectively prevent HFRS. However, the evolution and mutation of the virus pose challenges to this specific prevention and control measure. In this study, the levels of neutralizing antibodies against the vaccine strains and the current circulating virus strains in the panel of sera collected from confirmed HFRS patients at convalescent phase and adults who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv were evaluated. There are significant differences in the immunogenicity of cross protection induced by locally prevalent HV strains and vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi and SEOV L99), which suggested that the effectiveness of HFRSbiv may vary in different parts of China. Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by hantavirus remains a significant global public‑health burden (A1).
analysis.methods: A panel of sera was assembled from convalescent HFRS patients and individuals immunized with the bivalent inactivated HFRS vaccine, and neutralizing antibody titers against vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi, SEOV L99) and three epidemic strains (HTNV SX26, SEOV LN03, FJ‑17) were measured by an ELISA‑based microneutralization test (MN‑ELISA) (A6; A7).
analysis.results: Neutralizing antibodies were detected in all samples (A8); among 48 patients, 47.92% were HTNV‑infected, 27.08% SEOV‑infected, and 25% untypable (A9). Significant differences were observed between titers to vaccine versus epidemic strains (A10). For HTNV, geometric mean titers (GMT) were higher against vaccine strain 84FLi than epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:110.37 vs 1:223.04, P < 0.05) (A11‑A13). papers.title: Genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses: analysis code and derived data
papers.abstract: Analysis code and derived data from a study of genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and of nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses. The record contains, in nine data sections plus a code tree: 51 human tissue-specific codon adaptation index (CAI) weight tables built from Human Protein Atlas consensus expression; high-confidence tRNA gene sets and full-genome codon usage tables for five hantavirus reservoir hosts (Peromyscus maniculatus, Myodes glareolus, Talpa europaea, Sorex araneus, Sigmodon hispidus); protein-guided codon alignments of the nucleoprotein (S) and glycoprotein precursor (M) coding sequences of 22 hantavirus species (18 Orthohantavirus, two Thottimvirus, two Mobatvirus), with manifests, species label tables and alignment QC; the maximum-likelihood trees for both segments; the per-patient and per-segment open reading frame sets for the 28 patients of the 2018-2019 Epuyen Andes virus person-to-person outbreak; the pairwise divergence tables under three estimators, the exact species-label permutation tests, and the codeml control files and outputs for the branch models reported in this study; the within-species nucleotide-diversity table with its power and minimum-detectable-effect analysis; and the human codon usage and tRNA reference tables against which all CAI and codon co-adaptation values in this study are computed. The root README.md documents every section, gives the software versions used, and records three methodological cautions that are the parts of this work most likely to be reused: the tRNAscan-SE EukHighConfidenceFilter requirement, why a codon usage table must not be built from a few hundred GenBank CDS, and the per-amino-acid-family weight normalisation that a CAI implementation must apply. Scope note: this is a focused analysis package, not a project archive. Large third-party inputs (NCBI genome CDS sets, GenBank flatfile harvests, the Human Protein Atlas consensus matrix) are not redistributed; the manifests and download scripts included here retrieve them by accession. Derived per-sequence CAI scores are not deposited as tables, because they are recomputable from the deposited reference tables, sequences and code. Data are released under CC-BY-4.0. The code/ folder carries its own MIT licence (code/LICENCE_CODE.txt), matching the licence stated for the project repository.

papers.title_zh: 人际传播 安第斯病毒 爆发期间的基因组停滞,以及跨 汉坦病毒 的核蛋白和糖蛋白保守性:分析代码与衍生数据

analysis_zh.background: 该工作针对人际传播 安第斯病毒 爆发期间的基因组停滞进行研究,并考察跨 汉坦病毒 的核蛋白和糖蛋白保守性,涉及病毒进化与传播的相关议题。
analysis_zh.methods: 该仓库提供九个数据板块,包括人类组织特异性密码子适应指数表、高置信度 tRNA 基因集、五种储存宿主的全基因组密码子使用表、来自 22 种 汉坦病毒 物种的核蛋白 (S) 与糖蛋白前体 (M) 的蛋白引导密码子比对、最大似然系统发育树、28 名爆发患者的逐患者开放阅读框集合,以及多种分歧和 codeml 输出。
analysis_zh.results: 该套件包含三种估计方法下的成对分歧表、精确的物种标签置换检验以及分支模型 codeml 输出,同时提供种内核苷酸多样性表,并附有统计功效和最小可检测效应分析。
analysis_zh.contribution: 它提供可重复使用、文档完善的代码和数据套件,用于 汉坦病毒 密码子使用、tRNA 适应性和系统发育分析,支持未来的监测、进化及功能研究。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要层面的信息;未报告详细的实验设计、统计分析和作者解释,且数据集未包含衍生的 CAI 得分表。

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,涉及病毒特异性 CD8+ T 细胞,这些细胞既驱动病毒清除,也导致免疫病理 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究在肾综合征出血热患者和小鼠汉滩病毒感染模型中表征了HLA‐E/Qa‐1 限制的 CD8+ 调节性 T 细胞亚群,包括肽免疫和病毒挑战实验(A2)。
analysis_zh.results: CD8+ Tregs(CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+)在患者血液中显著减少,并表现出终末分化的抑制表型,与疾病严重程度相关(A3)。Qa‐1 结合的汉滩病毒肽免疫保护野生型小鼠免受肾免疫病理,而 Qa‐1 失活的 D227K 小鼠更有效清除病毒,但肾损伤更严重(A5)。Qa‐1 限制的 CD8+ Tregs 通过肽特异性、TGF‐β 依赖机制抑制效应 CD8+ 增殖(A6),D227K 突变改变了 Treg 表型并降低了抗原特异性抑制(A7)。总体而言,这些细胞以延迟病毒清除为代价限制病理(A8)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究发现一种新的 HLA‐E/Qa‐1 限制的 CD8+ Treg 轴,调节汉滩病毒感染中的免疫病理和病毒清除,提示其为肾综合征出血热及相关出血热的潜在治疗靶点(A9)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,限制了对实验设计、样本量和统计分析的细节(evidence_scope abstract_only)。

papers.title: Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany
papers.abstract: Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event.

Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The wild brown rats (M226, M268, and M186) from Rotterdam were selected for different levels of ORF1 sequence similarity to the 3 pet rat–derived sequences (Figure, panel A). The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. Dr. Mehl is a postdoctoral researcher at the Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut in Greifswald-Insel Riems, Germany. His research interests include the interplay between pathogen and host ecology, with a focus on small mammals. Acknowledgments We thank Dörte Kaufmann, Stephan Drewes, Elisabeth Striese, Stephanie Hübl, Silvia Schuparis, Christiane Klier, and Simon Dökel for their support. Ethical approval was not required for this investigation because it was conducted under the German Protection against Infection Act with the aim of investigating transmission routes and halting further spread of infection. All novel sequences were uploaded to GenBank (accession nos. PZ581217–22 and PZ583560–71). Funding was provided through the German Center for Infection Research, Thematical Translation Unit “Emerging Infections” (grant no. 01.808_00). C.M. acknowledges intramural funding by Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut, and R.J. acknowledges intramural funding by German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment. analysis.background: Pet rats are reservoirs of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including Seoul orthohantavirus and rat hepatitis E virus, which can infect humans.
analysis.methods: We screened 13 pet rats linked to human SEOV cases in Germany; liver RNA was tested by nested RT‑PCR for HEV/rHEV, confirmed by sequencing and real‑time RT‑PCR; serology used Luminex bead assay and Western blot; phylogenetic analysis compared sequences to GenBank.
analysis.results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats; the ORF1 sequences were 99.15–100% identical; serology showed 12/13 rats had rHEV antibodies, 3 also reacted to HEV‑3; phylogeny indicated close relation to a Rotterdam wild rat strain.
analysis.contribution: Findings suggest a single incursion of rHEV into pet rat populations and widespread circulation in breeding facilities, highlighting a potential zoonotic risk.
analysis.limitations: The study involved only 13 rats from a limited geographic area, so results may not generalize; sample size and scope were not reported in the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pet rats are reservoirs of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including Seoul orthohantavirus and rat hepatitis E virus, which can infect humans. Methods: We screened 13 pet rats linked to human SEOV cases in Germany; liver RNA was tested by nested RT‑PCR for HEV/rHEV, confirmed by sequencing and real‑time RT‑PCR; serology used Luminex bead assay and Western blot; phylogenetic analysis compared sequences to GenBank. Results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats; the ORF1 sequences were 99.15–100% identical; serology showed 12/13 rats had rHEV antibodies, 3 also reacted to HEV‑3; phylogeny indicated close relation to a Rotterdam wild rat strain. Contribution: Findings suggest a single incursion of rHEV into pet rat populations and widespread circulation in breeding facilities, highlighting a potential zoonotic risk. Limitations: The study involved only 13 rats from a limited geographic area, so results may not generalize; sample size and scope were not reported in the evidence.

papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Hantaan virus is endemic across Eurasia and poses a severe threat of renal failure and mortality.
analysis.methods: A systemic HTNV infection model was established in highly immunodeficient NCG mice; viral loads were quantified by qRT‑PCR and cellular tropism was mapped by immunofluorescence staining.
analysis.results: Infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained replication in kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver; HTNV showed organ‑specific tropism, primarily targeting renal fibroblasts/interstitial cells, pulmonary alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages, and multiple brain and ovary cell populations; co‑localization analyses suggested ITGB1, gC1qR, and ITGB2 as potential entry receptors in different organs.
analysis.contribution: The findings demonstrate that NCG mice provide a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available, limiting detail on experimental design, sample size, quantitative metrics, and broader contextual data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Hantaan virus is endemic across Eurasia and threatens renal failure and death. Methods: Researchers established a systemic HTNV infection model in highly immunodeficient NCG mice, measuring viral loads by qRT‑PCR and mapping cellular tropism via immunofluorescence. Results: Infected mice showed robust viremia and sustained replication in multiple organs, with distinct organ‑specific cellular tropism and potential entry receptors identified. Contribution: The study shows NCG mice are a valuable model for HTNV research. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided, restricting detail on methods and quantitative results.

papers.title_zh: 一种针对 汉滩病毒 的NCG小鼠模型揭示了系统性感染和器官特异性细胞嗜性。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,流行于欧亚大陆,构成严重的肾功能衰竭和死亡威胁。
analysis_zh.methods: 在高度免疫缺陷的NCG小鼠中建立了系统性汉滩病毒感染模型;通过qRT‐PCR定量病毒载量,并通过免疫荧光染色绘制细胞嗜性图谱。
analysis_zh.results: 感染的NCG小鼠出现强烈的血病毒血症,并在肾、肺、脾、生殖器官和肝中持续复制;汉滩病毒表现出器官特异性嗜性,主要靶向肾成纤维细胞/间质细胞、肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞,以及多种脑和卵巢细胞群;共定位分析提示ITGB1、gC1qR和ITGB2可能是不同器官中的进入受体。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究结果表明NCG小鼠为研究汉滩病毒复制和系统性传播提供了有价值的体内模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息,导致实验设计、样本量、定量指标以及更广泛背景数据的细节受限。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,流行于欧亚大陆,构成严重的肾功能衰竭和死亡威胁。 方法：在高度免疫缺陷的NCG小鼠中建立了系统性汉滩病毒感染模型;通过qRT‐PCR定量病毒载量,并通过免疫荧光染色绘制细胞嗜性图谱。 结果：感染的NCG小鼠出现强烈的血病毒血症,并在肾、肺、脾、生殖器官和肝中持续复制;汉滩病毒表现出器官特异性嗜性,主要靶向肾成纤维细胞/间质细胞、肺… 贡献：该研究结果表明NCG小鼠为研究汉滩病毒复制和系统性传播提供了有价值的体内模型。 局限：仅有摘要信息,导致实验设计、样本量、定量指标以及更广泛背景数据的细节受限。

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.
